stories.body: US President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran would begin Monday after he called off what he described as a planned massive attack, saying Iran and Gulf allies including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar believed a deal was possible. He said an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz could be followed by one on Iran's nuclear programme. Iran's Foreign Ministry denied that it planned to receive a US delegation or send officials to Washington, while Iranian media rejected Trump's claim that Tehran had asked the US to delay strikes. Tehran has said separate talks with Oman over a corridor through the Strait of Hormuz are nearing completion. Oil prices fell after Trump's announcement amid hopes of reduced disruption to Gulf energy supplies.
stories.headline: Trump says Iran talks will begin Monday, but Tehran denies any current negotiations

stories.body: Israeli strikes across Gaza killed at least 13 people according to Gaza's Civil Defence Authority, while other Palestinian health officials put the toll at 19. The dead included families in Gaza City, Khan Younis and Deir el-Balah, with several children reported among the casualties. The Israeli military said it was targeting militants and said it had killed Hamas operatives, including commanders. The attacks followed Hamas's acceptance of a proposed disarmament process under President Trump's Board of Peace, though Israel has said no deal has been reached to halt military action and remains sceptical that Hamas will surrender its weapons. Israeli officials have also conveyed concerns to Washington about the wider Gaza plan.
stories.headline: Israel strikes Gaza despite Hamas agreement on a disarmament plan

stories.body: Cuba's national electricity grid collapsed late Sunday, causing another island-wide blackout, state power operator UNE said without immediately identifying the cause or a restoration timetable. The failure follows three nationwide grid collapses within nine days in July and reflects an increasingly fragile system affected by fuel and spare-parts shortages, ageing thermoelectric plants and limited maintenance. Authorities generally restore service by first creating isolated networks for essential facilities such as hospitals, water systems and food services before reconnecting larger plants. The government blames US restrictions on fuel, finance and equipment, while critics also point to longstanding underinvestment and mismanagement.
stories.headline: Cuba hit by another nationwide blackout after grid failure

stories.body: At least 35 people were killed and several wounded when Sudanese army drones struck a traditional court in Garra al-Zawaya, a Rapid Support Forces-held village in North Darfur, according to the Emergency Lawyers rights group. Civilians had gathered under a tree with local leaders for hearings on local disputes when the afternoon attack occurred, and the court building was damaged. A witness said those killed included four tribal leaders and two RSF commanders. Sudan's war between the army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced millions and produced what the UN calls the world's largest humanitarian crisis.
stories.headline: Sudanese army drone strike kills 35 people at a court in Darfur, rights group says

stories.body: Japan and the United States confirmed a coordinated yen-buying intervention after the Japanese currency fell to a 40-year low, the first joint action of its kind since 2011. Tokyo's Finance Ministry said the move countered excessive volatility and disorderly yen movements, and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington could join further interventions. Bank of Japan data suggested Tokyo may have sold nearly $59 billion to buy yen in New York trading before the confirmed joint operation, while reports indicated the US action may have been worth $5 billion to $10 billion. The yen rose sharply following the announcement, though the stronger currency weighed on Japanese equities.
stories.headline: United States and Japan intervene jointly to support the yen in a rare move

stories.body: Fast-moving wildfires in and around Spokane, Washington, forced about 60,000 people to evacuate and destroyed at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures, authorities said. Roughly 5,000 homes were under evacuation orders as three separate fires spread rapidly in strong winds and exceptionally dry conditions. The fires remained uncontained on Sunday as crews confronted widespread damage across eastern Washington.
stories.headline: Wildfires around Spokane destroy hundreds of structures and force 60,000 evacuations

stories.body: Police say the suspect in Saturday's fatal shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound and acted alone. Investigators identified the gunman as 24-year-old Chad Williams. Police credited an off-duty officer and a civilian, both of whom fired at the suspect, with diverting him during the attack. Multiple people were killed and others wounded; authorities had not detailed the full casualty count in the information provided.
stories.headline: Authorities say Idaho In-N-Out shooter acted alone and died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound

stories.body: Maryland's legislature begins a special session Monday to consider a constitutional amendment that would give Democrats more latitude to redraw congressional districts ahead of the 2028 elections. Democrats currently hold seven of the state's eight US House seats and could seek to make the remaining Republican-held district more competitive. The measure would need voter approval before lawmakers could draw new maps. Supporters say the proposal responds to a changing national redistricting landscape after a recent Supreme Court decision weakened the Voting Rights Act, while state Republicans call it a partisan power grab. A previous attempt to redraw the Republican-held Eastern Shore district was struck down in 2022 as extreme partisan gerrymandering.
stories.headline: Maryland lawmakers consider partisan redistricting ahead of the 2028 elections

stories.body: Spain and the European Commission are due to meet EU interior ministers on Tuesday after a mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta exposed sharp divisions over migration policy. Thousands of people entered the Spanish enclave from Morocco by swimming or walking around the border breakwater, with local authorities estimating total arrivals at about 60,000 and El Periódico reporting 88 deaths. Spanish security forces said more than 53,000 people had returned voluntarily to Morocco by the end of Friday. Ceuta was caring for 862 unaccompanied migrant children, compared with its ordinary capacity of 29, according to the city's government. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares called the episode highly unusual and said Morocco had cooperated in preventing crossings and returning those who entered.
stories.headline: Ceuta migrant crisis leaves at least dozens dead as Spain and the EU confront the aftermath

stories.body: Spanish intelligence services have concluded that Moroccan authorities did not plan the mass movement of migrants toward Ceuta, but allowed it to proceed and used the international fallout for political advantage, according to El País. The influx of tens of thousands of people caught Spain's government off guard and left nearly 100 people dead while attempting the sea crossing, the report said. Moroccan authorities did not stop the crowd heading toward the Tarajal border crossing, according to the intelligence assessment.
stories.headline: Spanish intelligence concludes Morocco allowed and exploited the Ceuta migrant surge but did not plan it

stories.body: Spain's opposition People's Party has rejected negotiations with the government on a state pact against wildfires, instead planning to submit its own rural and forest assistance, recovery and prevention plan to parliament. The party's proposal, first presented by leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo in 2025, substantially overlaps with the government's climate-emergency pact, which was expanded after consultation with scientists, businesses, unions and civil-society groups. Despite those similarities, the two sides are not expected to reach an agreement.
stories.headline: People's Party rejects a state wildfire pact despite substantial overlap with the government's plan

stories.body: Spanish police have arrested a 17-year-old in Gipuzkoa who investigators describe as the leading figure in Spain for the online extremist network known as 764. A joint operation involving the Civil Guard, Mossos d'Esquadra and Ertzaintza links him to threats made between January and April against schools, town halls, libraries, public bodies and public figures, including Podemos MEP Irene Montero and commentator Sarah Santaolalla. Police say the international network targets vulnerable young people online through manipulation, sexual extortion, humiliation, self-harm and coercion. The teenager has been placed in preventive detention at a specialist centre, and investigators have identified at least two alleged victims, one in the Basque Country and one in Catalonia.
stories.headline: Police arrest 17-year-old alleged Spanish leader of violent extremist network 764

stories.body: The Kitchen espionage case has concluded and is awaiting judgment after examining recordings, text messages and a confession connected to an alleged 2013 operation within Spain's Interior Ministry to spy on former People's Party treasurer Luis Bárcenas. Bárcenas had become central to the Gürtel corruption case and a political threat to the governing party after reports of his Swiss fortune and the publication of papers documenting alleged party slush funds. The case concerns claims that senior officials used state resources in an effort to obtain information and materials from him.
stories.headline: Spain's Kitchen espionage case goes to judgment after evidence including recordings, messages and a confession

stories.body: The CGT union will proceed with an indefinite strike beginning Tuesday by Groundforce staff working in ground handling, check-in and boarding at Barcelona airport. The union, which holds a majority on the works committee, says the company has refused to negotiate with the strike committee and that employees face unsafe, undignified conditions, unsustainable workloads, high turnover, excessive overtime and inadequate breaks and training. The stoppage could affect airlines served by Groundforce, including Air Europa, Lufthansa, Air France, KLM, Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines, United Airlines and others.
stories.headline: Barcelona airport ground staff maintain an indefinite strike beginning Tuesday

stories.body: Catalonia's government says it has redesigned 170 administrative procedures and plans to simplify more than 200 during the current term, with an estimated annual saving of more than six million hours for residents. The reforms, under the Catgirem programme, cover health, education, business, agriculture and justice, using digital forms, automation and data-sharing to avoid unnecessary visits and requests for information already held by the administration. Examples include digital consent for certain medical procedures through La Meva Salut, a simpler registration process for domestic partnerships, digital Catalan-language certificates and improved reporting of agricultural damage caused by wildlife. The government has invested €11.3 million in the initiative and aims to reach 210 reformed procedures.
stories.headline: Catalonia moves to simplify more than 200 administrative procedures

stories.body: Police safely removed three anti-aircraft artillery shells found in an apartment on Carrer de Nàpols in Barcelona's Sagrada Família area. A resident alerted the Mossos d'Esquadra on July 31 while the home was being cleared. Two shells were 76mm rounds measuring about 80cm long, and the third was a 37mm round about 40cm long; police said all were in good condition. Bomb-disposal specialists collected the munitions for safe destruction. Mossos urged anyone who finds a suspected explosive device not to touch or move it and to call 112.
stories.headline: Three anti-aircraft shells found inside an Eixample apartment are safely removed

stories.body: Barcelona hotels expect occupancy close to or above 90% in August, with more visitors making last-minute reservations amid uncertainty linked to the Middle East conflict. Hotel operators say August, once a weaker month for the city, has benefited from international tourism and beach travel, with stays tending to be longer and more family-oriented. Tourist apartments expect average occupancy of about 86%, with the United States, United Kingdom, France, Italy and Spain among the main markets. The outlook follows a record first half of 2026, when Barcelona hotels hosted 4.49 million guests, up 3.9% year on year, and recorded 10.65 million overnight stays.
stories.headline: Barcelona hotels expect August occupancy near or above 90% amid growing last-minute bookings
